newsitem.title: UK: Possible EMU delay seen as mixed blessing for UK.
newsitem.headline: Possible EMU delay seen as mixed blessing for UK.

text.p: Uncertainty about the prospects for a single European currency could prove a mixed blessing for Britain economically, but the country's new Labour government might secretly welcome a delay, economists said on Thursday.

Sterling strengthened against the deutschemark as traders saw both the British currency and the dollar as "safe havens" amid the confusion caused by a bitter row between the German government and the Bundesbank.
The German central bank opposes government plans to revalue gold reserves to fill a budget shortfall and enable Germany to qualify to join the single currency.
Prime Minister Tony Blair's government maintained a public silence on events in Germany.

But former Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said he supported the Bundesbank and believed a delay in the start-date for EMU beyond 1999 was now both sensible and likely.
"It strengthens all the arguments for delay," Clarke, the opposition's most committed Europhile, told BBC television.

"No-one should go into a single currency unless the convergence criteria are genuinely met. There will be no advantages if countries go ahead on the basis of accounting devices. What matters is the underlying reality."
John Redwood, one of Clarke's "Eurosceptic" rivals in the contest to succeed John Major as Conservative leader, described Bonn's gold revaluation plans as "a fiddle which will not work."
Economists said confusion about the fate of economic and monetary union (EMU) would make Britain, which negotiated an "opt-out" clause, more attractive to foreign investors.

"Britain is well placed anyway on domestic grounds as a large liquid market with a safe government -- safe in the sense that it is not going to fall," said Alison Cottrell, chief economist at Paine Webber. "That's a rare commodity in Europe."
An influx of funds from overseas would make it cheaper for the government to borrow money and could boost share prices.
The downside is that a further appreciation in the already strong pound would make life tougher for British exporters, who are struggling to sell their goods abroad.

The gold row in Germany and the possibility that French voters may elect a left-wing government less committed to rigorous preconditions for EMU raise the possibility that the start-date for the single currency may be delayed.
It is thought highly unlikely that Britain would join in 1999 if the project started as planned.

Nevertheless, analysts believe the Blair government might welcome a delay in having to confront this highly contentious issue, which would enable it to devote more time to its ambitious domestic agenda.
"Blair's ideal world is probably one in which there is no EMU to join or not join in 1999," Cottrell said. "The delay could be beneficial from a policy coherence point of view in Britain."
"If there is a credible delay for two years, Britain might well then be talked of as being in there."
Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Markets, believes the row in Germany is unlikely to materially alter the opinions of new Chancellor Gordon Brown.
Although he is cautious in his public pronouncements and has warned of "formidable obstacles" in the path of EMU, Brown is generally thought to favour British participation.
"Brown's position is based on a philosophy that says if you have a single trade area next to you, it is dangerous to be outside it," Juckes said.
He believes events in Germany will lead to one of two possible outcomes -- "Either there is an EMU delay or there is a soft euro, a fudged EMU."

If the single currency started on shaky foundations, it would be in Britain's interests to wait and see if it succeeds. But Juckes believes the attractions of being in could still outweigh the prospect of being outside.

"If Europe starts out on a deliberately devaluationist tack, then part of the downside of not being in is that you would get a strong currency. We will be tempted with low interest rates and a softer currency if we go in."
